1.text: *Alif-Lãm-Mĩm.* Three letters, no verb, no sentence, and no meaning that any dictionary will give you. This is the first verse of the longest sūrah in the Qurʾān, and it is not a statement at all. Maʿārif-ul-Qurʾān explains the form before anything else. Several sūrahs open with a combination of Arabic letters — *Ḥā-Mīm*, *Alif-Lām-Mīm-Ṣād*, and so on. Each letter is pronounced on its own, without a vowel added after it, which is why the technical term for them is *muqaṭṭaʿāt*, isolated letters. Tazkīrul Qurʾān counts them: they appear at the beginning of twenty-nine chapters, and some of them became the names of the sūrahs themselves — *Ṭā-Hā*, *Yā-Sīn*, *Ṣād*, *Qāf*. **What the scholars said about them.** There are three positions, and it matters which one you hold. Some commentators took them to be the names of the sūrahs they head. Others took them to be symbols of the Divine Names. Tanwīr al-Miqbās preserves this line of reading from Ibn ʿAbbās in several forms: *Alif* stands for Allah, *Lām* for the angel Jibrīl, and *Mīm* for Muḥammad; or *Alif* stands for Allah's blessings, *Lām* for His kindness and *Mīm* for His dominion; or they are the opening letters of three of His Names — Allah, al-Laṭīf, al-Majīd. Some held it is an oath He has taken. The majority position is different, and Maʿārif is explicit that this is where most of the Companions, the Tābiʿūn and the later authoritative scholars landed: the isolated letters are symbols whose meaning is known to Allah alone, or was entrusted to the Prophet ﷺ as a confidence not to be passed on. The evidence for that reading is negative and strong — no explanation of these letters was ever reported from him. Al-Qurṭubī adopted this view. Al-Jalālayn states it in a single line: God knows best what He means by these letters. **Why they are there at all.** Al-Mukhtaṣar gives the functional answer. The letters have no meaning in themselves, but they have a purpose. Since there is divine wisdom in everything in the Qurʾān, these letters point to the miracle of a book made out of the same letters that make up ordinary human speech. And he adds an observation you can check: when a sūrah opens with letters like these, it is usually followed by a verse about the Qurʾān itself. That is exactly what happens here. The very next verse is *This is the Book.* So the letters are a challenge before the claim. Here are the components — the alphabet you already use — and here is what has been built from them. **What Ibn Kathīr does instead.** Worth knowing: Ibn Kathīr does not spend his entry on the letters. He opens with the merits of the sūrah itself, and the reports he gathers are worth having. In the Musnad of Aḥmad, Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim, at-Tirmidhī and an-Nasāʾī, Abū Hurayrah reports that the Prophet ﷺ said: *Do not turn your houses into graves. Verily, Shayṭān does not enter the house where Sūrat al-Baqarah is recited.* At-Tirmidhī graded it ḥasan ṣaḥīḥ. Ibn Masʿūd said: *Shayṭān flees from the house where Sūrat al-Baqarah is heard.* An-Nasāʾī collected it in *al-Yawm wal-Laylah*, and al-Ḥākim in his *Mustadrak*, calling its chain authentic while noting that the two Ṣaḥīḥs did not carry it. Ad-Dārimī records from ash-Shaʿbī, from Ibn Masʿūd: *Whoever recites ten verses from Sūrat al-Baqarah in a night, Shayṭān will not enter his house that night; whoever recites it during a day in his house, Shayṭān will not enter that house for three days.* Abū al-Qāsim aṭ-Ṭabarānī, Ibn Ḥibbān in his Ṣaḥīḥ, and Ibn Marduwayh all carry it. Al-Bukhārī records Usayd ibn Ḥuḍayr reciting al-Baqarah at night with his horse tethered beside him, and something approaching that he could not make out. The Prophet ﷺ told him: *Those were the angels. They came close to hear your voice, and had you kept reading, people would have been able to see them when morning came.* A sūrah that opens with three unexplained letters, and whose opening report is about what happens in a room when it is read aloud.

2.text: *This is the Book! There is no doubt about it—a guide for those mindful ˹of Allah˺.* The verse makes a claim about itself, and then narrows who benefits from it. Both halves deserve attention. **Why "this" and not "that".** Maʿārif raises the difficulty directly. The Arabic reads *dhālika'l-kitāb*, and *dhālika* — *that* — is a pronoun used to point at something distant. But the Book being referred to is the Qurʾān, which is right here in front of the reader. The demonstrative seems wrong. Maʿārif's reading is that it is not wrong but deliberate. The pronoun points back to the prayer at the end of al-Fātiḥah — *Guide us along the Straight Path.* That request has now been answered, and this Book is the answer. The distance in the pronoun is the distance between asking and receiving. Al-Jalālayn reads the same feature differently: the demonstrative is there to glorify the Book. Both readings agree that the choice of word is doing work. **"There is no doubt about it".** Ibn Kathīr's entry is largely a roll call. As-Suddī reports that Abū Mālik and Abū Ṣāliḥ transmitted from Ibn ʿAbbās, and Murrah al-Hamadhānī from Ibn Masʿūd, along with several other Companions, that *in which there is no rayb* means *about which there is no doubt.* Abū ad-Dardāʾ, Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, Saʿīd ibn Jubayr, Abū Mālik, Nāfiʿ, ʿAṭāʾ, Abū al-ʿĀliyah, ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas, Muqātil ibn Ḥayyān, as-Suddī, Qatādah and Ismāʿīl ibn Abī Khālid all said the same. Then Ibn Kathīr records Ibn Abī Ḥātim: *I do not know of any disagreement over this explanation.* For a word as loaded as this one, that is unusual. Some scholars read the sentence as carrying a prohibition rather than a description — *do not doubt the Qurʾān.* **Where to pause when reciting.** Ibn Kathīr notes a live disagreement among the reciters. Some pause after *there is no doubt* and then continue *in which there is guidance for those mindful of Allah.* He judges it better to pause after *in which there is no doubt*, because on that reading *guidance* becomes an attribute of the Book itself rather than merely something contained in it — and that carries the stronger meaning. It is a small point about breath, and it changes what the verse asserts. **Who the mindful are.** Ibn ʿAbbās is recorded twice on *al-muttaqīn*. First: *the believers who avoid associating partners with Allah and who work in His obedience.* Second: *those who fear Allah's punishment, which would result if they abandoned the guidance they recognise and know, and who hope in Allah's mercy by believing in what He revealed.* Fear and hope, again, as in 1:5. Qatādah simply points forward: *al-muttaqīn* are the people Allah describes in the next verse — *who believe in the unseen and establish prayer.* Ibn ʿAbbās and Ibn Masʿūd render the phrase as *a light for those who have taqwā.* **Why only they.** This is the part most easily misread. The verse does not say the Book is unclear and only the pious can decode it. Tazkīrul Qurʾān explains the mechanism: there is no doubt that the Qurʾān is a book of guidance, but it guides only those who are sincere in searching for truth and anxious to be guided. The search is already in human nature; what is required is to uncover it. Al-Mukhtaṣar puts the claim and the condition together: this is the Qurʾān, in which there is nothing of any doubt, neither in its origin nor in its meaning — and it guides those who are mindful of Allah to the way that leads to Him. Tanwīr al-Miqbās adds a harder edge, offering among its readings that there is no doubt it has come from God: believe in it and be guided, or do not, and face the consequence. And one of its readings ties the verse to the earlier scriptures — that there is no doubt the description and traits of Muḥammad ﷺ are to be found in the Torah and the Gospel, which the next verse then takes up.

3.text: *Who believe in the unseen, establish prayer, and donate from what We have provided for them.* Three clauses, and they are not a list of duties so much as a map of where belief shows up: in what you accept, in what you do with your body, and in what you do with your money. **What faith means.** Ibn Kathīr opens on the word itself and lets the early authorities disagree. Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī transmits through al-ʿAlāʾ ibn al-Musayyib ibn Rāfiʿ, from Abū Isḥāq, from Abū al-Aḥwaṣ, from ʿAbdullāh: *Īmān is to trust.* ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah reports from Ibn ʿAbbās that *who have faith* means *they trust.* Maʿmar reports from az-Zuhrī: *Īmān is deeds.* Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī reports from ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas: *they have faith* means *they fear Allah.* Four definitions from four authorities, and Ibn Kathīr does not simply pick one. He notes that linguistically, in the absolute sense, *īmān* means trust, and the Qurʾān uses it that way — *he trusts in Allah and trusts in the believers* (9:61), and Yūsuf's brothers saying *you will never believe us even when we speak the truth* (12:17). Some scholars explained *īmān* as *khashyah*, fear of Allah. Then he gives Ibn Jarīr's synthesis, which is the one worth keeping: the preferred view is that they are described as having faith in the unseen by tongue, deed and creed together. *Īmān* is a general term covering affirmation of Allah, His Books and His Messengers, and then realising that affirmation by acting on what the tongue has said. Belief, affirmation and action are not three candidates for the meaning. They are one thing described from three sides. **What the unseen is.** Ibn Kathīr says plainly that the Salaf differed on this and that all their explanations are correct, pointing at the same general meaning. Abū Jaʿfar ar-Rāzī quotes ar-Rabīʿ ibn Anas reporting from Abū al-ʿĀliyah: *They believe in Allah, His angels, His Books, His Messengers, the Last Day, His Paradise, His Fire, and in the meeting with Him. All of this is the unseen.* Qatādah ibn Diʿāmah said the same. Tanwīr al-Miqbās lists more concretely: that which is hidden from them, such as Paradise, Hell, the Bridge, the Scale, the Resurrection and the Reckoning. It records two further readings — that they believe in the unseen revealed in the Qurʾān as well as in what is not revealed in it, and that the unseen referred to is Allah Himself. Al-Jalālayn is shortest: what is hidden from them of the Resurrection, Paradise and the Fire. **Establishing prayer, not merely performing it.** The translation says *establish*, and the Arabic is stronger than *perform.* Tanwīr al-Miqbās unpacks it: they complete the five prescribed prayers, including the ablution that precedes them, the bowing and the prostrations, and what is obligatory in them with respect to their appointed times. Al-Jalālayn compresses the same idea: they perform it giving it its due. Establishing a prayer means it is built into the structure of the day rather than fitted around it. **Spending from what was given.** Note the framing in the verse itself: *from what We have provided for them.* Ownership is already qualified before the spending is mentioned. Tanwīr al-Miqbās reads it as giving charity from the wealth Allah gave them, and records the narrower reading that it means the obligatory poor-due, zakāh. Al-Jalālayn: they expend in obedience to God. **How the three clauses connect.** Tazkīrul Qurʾān offers the most coherent account of why these three belong together, tracing each back to an instinct that precedes it. True searching and true finding are the early and later stages of a single journey; whoever searches for truth unlocks faculties in himself that were closed. The vague yearnings of human nature then begin to receive a definite response, and that awakening is an attempt to discern the world of meanings behind the world of forms. When that leads to a discovery, it becomes faith in the unseen. What began as an urge to submit to some higher power takes the form of bowing to the Almighty. What began as a wish to sacrifice oneself for a greater good takes the form of spending one's wealth in God's cause. The verse is not listing requirements. It is describing what one inward movement looks like once it has become three outward habits.

4.text: *And who believe in what has been revealed to you ˹O Prophet˺ and what was revealed before you, and have sure faith in the Hereafter.* The previous verse described belief in the unseen generally. This one names its two objects — revelation, including revelation that came before this Book — and then adds a word the previous verse did not use. **No distinction between the messengers.** Ibn ʿAbbās's explanation, recorded by Ibn Kathīr, is direct: *They believe in what Allah sent you with, and in what the previous messengers were sent with. They do not distinguish between them, nor do they reject what they brought from their Lord.* Al-Mukhtaṣar states the same with the phrase that carries the weight: they believe in what Allah sent down to you, O Prophet, and in what He revealed to all the other prophets before you, *without distinction.* That clause excludes a specific failure — accepting some prophets and discarding others — which is precisely the charge the Qurʾān will press later in this sūrah. **Who this verse is about.** Maʿārif preserves a report from the Companions ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd and ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAbbās that gives the verse a historical setting. In the Prophet's lifetime, the God-fearing were of two kinds: those who had been polytheists and disbelievers and then accepted Islam, and those who had been People of the Book and embraced Islam later. The preceding verse describes the first group; this verse describes the second. That is why belief in the earlier Books is mentioned here specifically. According to the ḥadīth Maʿārif cites, the second group earns a double reward — first for believing in and following the earlier Books before the Qurʾān came to supersede them, and second for believing in and following the Qurʾān when it arrived as the final Book. Maʿārif adds the standing obligation: it remains obligatory for every Muslim to believe in the earlier divine Books. **Ibn Kathīr's structural note.** He records Mujāhid's mapping of the whole opening: *Four verses at the beginning of Sūrat al-Baqarah describe the believers, two describe the disbelievers, and thirteen describe the hypocrites.* Four, two, thirteen. The sūrah's opening is not a preamble; it is a table of contents for the human types it will spend its length on. Ibn Kathīr then widens the scope of the four verses: they are general and include every believer — Arab or non-Arab, a person of a previous scripture or not, jinn or human. And he draws an inference worth noting: if believers among the People of the Book gain two rewards, other Muslims whose faith is firmer may gain a reward equal to those two. **The word that changes: certainty.** The verse ends *and in the Hereafter they are certain* — and *certain* is a stronger word than *believe.* Al-Jalālayn's rendering shows the difference is not decorative. Ibn Kathīr lists what that certainty covers: the resurrection, the standing on the Day of Resurrection, Paradise, the Fire, the reckoning and the Scale that weighs deeds, the mīzān. Al-Mukhtaṣar: a definite belief in the Afterlife, with its rewards and punishments. So the two verses run: belief in the unseen, then certainty about the unseen. The first is acceptance of what cannot be verified; the second is that acceptance having settled into conviction. The believers described here have already made that crossing, which is why the very next verse announces they are guided — not that they are trying.

5.text: *It is they who are ˹truly˺ guided by their Lord, and it is they who will be successful.* Four verses have described a type of person. This one closes the description, and it is deliberately short — fifty-six words in the plan where the verses around it run to nine hundred. Brevity is the point. After four verses of qualification, the verdict needs no elaboration. **Note what the verse does not say.** It does not say they will be guided. It says they *are* upon guidance. The Arabic construction — *ulāʾika ʿalā hudā* — puts them already standing on it, not moving towards it. Guidance is not the reward promised at the end; it is the condition they are in. Ibn Kathīr's entry is the shortest of the seven and stays close to the text: *On guidance* means they are following a light, guidance and insight from Allah; *and they are the successful* means in this world and the Hereafter. **"Upon" guidance, not "in" it.** Tanwīr al-Miqbās expands the preposition: these people, who have these traits, are on guidance from their Lord — they enjoy favour, mercy and clear exposition that has come down from Him. It adds a second reading: the successful are those who have grasped and found what they were seeking, and have escaped the evil of what they were fleeing. That pairing is the shape of the whole promise. Success here is defined twice, once as attainment and once as escape. Al-Jalālayn gives the same two halves in the plainest terms: those described in this way are upon guidance from their Lord, and they are the ones who will prosper — meaning they will succeed in entering Paradise and be saved from the Fire. Maʿārif compresses it to a single sentence: those who possess these qualities are on the path of guidance and will be successful in this world and the next, gaining what they desire and being saved from what they fear. **Why the demonstrative is repeated.** *It is they* … *and it is they.* The Arabic repeats *ulāʾika*, and the repetition restricts the claim in the same way the fronted object did in 1:5. It is not guidance in general that is being described, and not success in general. It is these people, and they specifically. That restriction is what makes the next verse land. The sūrah has just said who succeeds; the very next verse turns to those for whom warning and non-warning have become identical, and the contrast is the argument. **Where the first unit ends.** Mujāhid's count, recorded by Ibn Kathīr at 2:4, put four verses to the believers. This is the fourth — the conclusion rather than a fifth quality. The description is complete: belief in the unseen, prayer, spending, belief in all revelation, certainty about the Hereafter. Then the verdict. Tanwīr al-Miqbās records a reading that identifies the group historically rather than typologically: these are the Companions of Muḥammad ﷺ. The verse was revealed among people who could see the description being lived out beside them, which is why it needed no explanation when it first arrived.

6.text: *As for those who persist in disbelief, it is the same whether you warn them or not—they will never believe.* The sūrah turns abruptly. Four verses on the guided, and now two on those for whom guidance has stopped being available. The shift is the argument: the same Book produces opposite results in different people, and verse two already told you why. **What disbelief means here.** Ibn Kathīr gives the root sense first: *those who disbelieve* means those who covered the truth and hid it. The word is not about absence of conviction. It is about something present being concealed. That matters for reading the rest of the verse. These are not people who have never encountered the claim. They are people who have, and have covered it over. **The Prophet's own reluctance.** Ibn Kathīr records through ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭalḥah, from Ibn ʿAbbās, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ was eager for all people to believe and to follow the guidance he had been sent with. That report explains the verse's tone. The statement that warning makes no difference is not delivered coldly. It is addressed to a man who wanted the opposite and kept warning anyway, and it exists to release him from an expectation he could not meet. Al-Jalālayn draws the practical conclusion bluntly: it is alike to them whether you have warned them or not, they do not believe, *as God knows very well — so do not hope that they will believe.* Al-Jalālayn names examples: the likes of Abū Jahl and Abū Lahab. It also records a grammatical note on the recitation of *a-andhartahum*, whether both hamzas are pronounced or the second is softened into an alif, with or without an inserted alif between them. And it defines the word itself: *indhār*, warning, is to give knowledge of something while simultaneously instilling an element of fear. Warning is not neutral information. It is information delivered with its consequences attached. **Stubbornness, not ignorance.** Al-Mukhtaṣar's reading is short and specific: those who reject what Allah revealed to His Messenger continue on the wrong path *in their stubbornness*. So it makes no difference whether you warn them or not. Tanwīr al-Miqbās makes the same point about volition: whether you instil fear in them by means of the Qurʾān or you do not, it is all one for them — they do not *want* to believe. It adds a second reading, that they will not believe because it stands in Allah's knowledge. **Why Maʿārif places this verse here.** Maʿārif's account of the sūrah's structure is the clearest available. Having affirmed the Qurʾān as the Book of guidance beyond all doubt, the first five verses describe those who benefit from it fully — the *muʾminūn* or *muttaqūn* — and set out the qualities that distinguish them. The next fifteen verses describe those who refuse this guidance and oppose it out of spite and blind malice. And in the Prophet's time there were two distinct groups of them. One came out into open hostility and rejection, and the Qurʾān calls them *kāfirūn*. The other, out of moral weakness and greed, did not have the courage to say what they thought, and took the route of deceit and duplicity — telling the Muslims they believed, while working against them. Two verses for the first group, thirteen for the second. The hypocrites get more than six times the attention, which tells you where the sūrah thinks the real danger lies. **Why truth is refused.** Tazkīrul Qurʾān gives the social mechanism, and it is the most uncomfortable part of this verse. However clear the call of truth may be, it can only be understood and accepted by a mind that is open to it. God's inaudible call in the universe, and the preacher's audible expression of it, cannot touch closed minds. Then the harder observation: where a society is rigidly bound by age-old convention, people are less concerned with opening their minds to divine realities than with protecting the vested interests of the existing system. The preacher, as God's emissary, is neither a representative nor a supporter of that structure. His call is new and unfamiliar, and it presents itself as a threat to material security. On that reading, verse six is not describing a theological failure. It is describing what happens when truth arrives in a place where people have something to lose.

7.text: *Allah has sealed their hearts and their hearing, and their sight is covered. They will suffer a tremendous punishment.* Verse six said warning makes no difference. This verse says why — and the explanation is the difficult part, because the sealing is attributed to Allah. **What the sealing is.** Ibn Kathīr gathers the early explanations and they converge on a process rather than an arbitrary act. As-Suddī: *khatama Allāh* means *Allah has sealed.* Qatādah gives the sequence: *Shayṭān gained control of them when they obeyed him; therefore Allah sealed their hearts, their hearing and their sight, and they could neither see the guidance nor hear it, comprehend it or understand it.* Obedience first, sealing after. Ibn Jurayj reports from Mujāhid: *A stamp. It occurs when sin resides in the heart and surrounds it from all sides, and this submersion of the heart in sin constitutes a stamp — meaning a seal.* Mujāhid also ranked the stages, through ʿAbdullāh ibn Kathīr: *the stain is not as bad as the stamp, and the stamp is not as bad as the lock, which is the worst type.* Al-Aʿmash describes Mujāhid demonstrating it with his hand — the heart held open like a palm, then closed. And Mujāhid connected it to the *rān* of 83:14, the covering that grows over a heart. None of these describe a verdict handed down from nowhere. They describe a heart that has been progressively closed by its own choices until the closing is complete. **The consensus, and the prayer that answers it.** Al-Qurṭubī's statement, quoted by Ibn Kathīr, settles the doctrine: the ummah has agreed that Allah has described Himself as sealing and closing the hearts of the disbelievers *as a punishment for their disbelief.* He cites the parallel verse — *Nay, Allah has set a seal upon their hearts because of their disbelief* (4:155) — where the cause is stated explicitly. Al-Qurṭubī then does something telling. He immediately cites the Prophet's supplication, *O You who changes the hearts, make our hearts firm upon Your religion*, and the ḥadīth of Ḥudhayfah in the Ṣaḥīḥ: *Trials are presented to the hearts as the straws of a woven mat are laid one after another…* ending with a heart that no longer recognises what is right or refuses what is wrong. The sealing is real, and it is also reversible enough to be prayed against. That is why the Prophet ﷺ prayed it. **How the punishment works in this life.** Maʿārif's contribution is the most searching. These verses tell us that the Hereafter is where the real punishment for disbelief is received — but some punishment arrives in this world, and it can take a graver form than pain. The divine favour that enables a person to reform himself is withdrawn. Then, with no thought for how the deeds will be assessed on the Day of Judgment, he keeps growing in disobedience until he loses even the awareness that what he is doing is evil. Maʿārif quotes the elders: one punishment for an evil deed is the evil deed that follows it, and one reward for a good deed is the good deed that follows it. He then cites the ḥadīth of the black dot. When a man commits a sin, a black dot appears on his heart, and that first dot disturbs him the way a smudge on white cloth always does. But if instead of seeking pardon he commits a second, another dot appears — and so with every new sin, until the covering is complete. That is verse seven from the inside. The seal is not applied at once. It is built. **What the three faculties mean.** The verse names three, and they are not redundant. Al-Mukhtaṣar separates them cleanly: Allah has sealed their hearts, locking their falsehood inside; He has sealed their hearing, so that they neither listen to nor accept the truth; and He has placed a cover over their eyes, so that they do not see the truth in its clarity. Al-Jalālayn gives each its function: a seal on the hearts, impressing on them and making certain that no good enters; something deposited in the hearing so they cannot profit from the truth they hear; a veil over the eyes so they do not see it. Affection, attention and perception — the three ways a person takes truth in, all closed. **Who it was about, and what comes next.** Tanwīr al-Miqbās records two identifications: particular Jews of Madīnah — Kaʿb ibn al-Ashraf, Ḥuyayy ibn Akhṭab and Judayy ibn Akhṭab — or the idolaters of Makkah, ʿUtbah ibn Rabīʿah, Shaybah ibn Rabīʿah and al-Walīd ibn al-Mughīrah. Al-Mukhtaṣar closes by turning the page, and his note is the hinge into the next thirteen verses: after describing the disbelievers, who are at fault inside and out, Allah describes the hypocrites, who appear good on the outside and are not so within. The sūrah has now sorted people into the guided and the sealed. The third group — the ones who look like the first and are the second — is what it spends the next thirteen verses on.
